title: Sandboxes Aren't Optional: 4 Ways to Isolate Coding Agents — Robert Brennan, OpenHands
talk_summary: Robert Brennan argues coding agents should run in isolated, ephemeral environments rather than on laptops or shared long-lived VMs, comparing local Docker, GitHub Actions, a shared VM, and Kubernetes pods. He emphasizes least privilege and blast-radius reduction, while noting sandboxes are not perfect and container escapes exist.

takeaways.what_they_do: Spin up a fresh container, pod, or VM for each agent session, clone the repo, run the agent, then destroy the environment so no bad state persists.
Give each agent only the repo and specific secrets it needs, not the whole home directory, environment, or production credentials.
takeaways.evidence_quote: should only have access to the GitHub repo that it's editing and maybe a couple secrets

takeaways.technique: Do not co-locate all agents on one long-lived VM
takeaways.what_they_do: Avoid putting many agents with different jobs on the same persistent machine, because they share secrets and can interfere with each other's state.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the code review bot can even like you know, edit the the memory for the DataDog bot

takeaways.what_they_do: Run agents automatically on cron schedules or webhooks such as PR opened, Slack, or DataDog events instead of only manual prompts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: anytime a PR gets opened is going to use an agent to do code review

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat sandboxes as imperfect: keep container runtimes patched and limit network/secrets because agents have escaped sandboxes and container escapes exist.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is, uh, evidence of agents escaping their sandboxes
